title: The Nasdaq-100 Had Its Worst Week in 18 Months. History Says the Following Year Has Usually Been Strong.
detail:
The Nasdaq-100 Had Its Worst Week in 18 Months. History Says the Following Year Has Usually Been Strong.
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Sat, October 24, 2026 at 11:27 AM EDT 5 min read
QQQ
SMH
NVDA

Trading disclosure

The Nasdaq-100 fell about 5.5% in the week ending Oct. 16. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ), the exchange-traded fund that tracks the index, dropped around the same amount. That was the index's worst week since the one ending April 4, 2025, when it lost almost 10%.

Chip stocks did a lot of the damage. The VanEck Semiconductor ETF fell around 10% that week, its largest weekly drop since April 2025, while other stocks linked to artificial intelligence (AI) slid, too.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Investors also worried about how much tech firms are borrowing to cover AI-related capital spending, and hotter-than-expected inflation numbers and oil over $100 a barrel added to the pressure.

I wanted to see what QQQ did in the year after weeks like this one, so I dug through its daily prices, which begin in 1999. As I write this, the fund trades near $724, or about 5% under its record close of about $760 on Oct. 6.

Image source: Getty Images.

QQQ nearly always climbed over the next year

To stop one bad spell from being counted several times, I only counted the first week with a loss of 4% or more in any 30-day window. Since 2010, 26 of these weeks have had a full 12 months to play out. (Two other drops in 2026, in June and July, are too recent to score.)

QQQ was higher a year later after 25 of the 26. The median gain was around 22%, based on price alone, before dividends. The latest case, the week that ended April 4, 2025, was followed by a gain of about 38% in the next year. And in late February 2020, when the pandemic spread, QQQ lost about 11% in a week and then climbed about 53% in the following year.

Of course, QQQ, which is loaded with growth stocks, has risen in most years since 2010 whatever sort of week came before. Taking any week since 2010 at random, the fund ended the next 12 months up in around nine out of 10 cases, with a median gain near 21%.

In other words, those bad weeks were usually followed by an ordinary year for QQQ. And an ordinary year for the fund has been a pretty good one since 2010.

The 2022 exception

The only miss was in early 2022. QQQ dropped around 4.5% in the week ending Jan. 7, 2022, and a year later it was down around 29%.

That week turned out to be early in a long slide. The Federal Reserve started lifting its benchmark interest rate from near zero in March 2022, and by December, its target range was 4.25% to 4.5%. Higher interest rates can drag on stock valuations, especially for firms whose profits are expected to come years from now. The Nasdaq-100 dropped around 33% that year, its worst calendar year since 2008.

title: Schwab's Dividend ETF Just Closed at a Record Without Owning a Single "Magnificent Seven" Stock
detail:
Schwab's Dividend ETF Just Closed at a Record Without Owning a Single "Magnificent Seven" Stock
Daniel Sparks, The Motley Fool
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 1:44 PM EDT 5 min read
QQQ
SCHD
NVDA
Explore stocks on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

The Schwab U.S. Dividend Equity ETF (NYSEMKT:SCHD) finished Thursday, Oct. 22, at $35.40, the highest close in the popular dividend fund's history. This beat its old record of $35.21 from Aug. 24, and it leaves the fund up around 29% from where it ended 2025.

That same day, the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) lost about 3%. And as of this writing, the Nasdaq-100 fund has slid around 7% since Oct. 6, but the dividend fund has risen about 8%.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

It did that without the stocks that have led the market for much of the last few years. As of Oct. 13, not one of its 102 holdings belonged to the so-called "Magnificent Seven" -- Apple, Microsoft, Nvidia, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Tesla.

With dividends, it's also topped all of those seven stocks in 2026. I think what that mix means for an owner matters more than the record itself.

Image source: Getty Images.

The 10-year rule

The fund tracks the Dow Jones U.S. Dividend 100 Index, which starts with a basic rule. A company needs to have paid dividends for at least 10 years running. Of the stocks that pass, the lower-yielding half is cut. The rest are ranked by a score based on cash flow relative to total debt, return on equity, dividend yield and five-year dividend growth.

The first rule keeps out four of the seven. Amazon and Tesla don't pay dividends, and Meta and Alphabet just began paying them in 2024.

Apple, Microsoft and Nvidia have longer dividend records, of course. But each yields under 1% as I write. And with yields that low, they probably don't get past the yield cut.

That leaves the fund leaning elsewhere. As of Sept. 30, consumer staples and healthcare stocks made up around 39% of the fund and energy stocks about 15%. Tech stocks were only about 12%.

A steady core

The index reshuffles once a year, in March, so today's fund isn't quite what an owner held in January. But a core of big positions stuck around and they had a huge year.

Texas Instruments (NASDAQ:TXN), ConocoPhillips, Chevron, Merck, Amgen and Coca-Cola together made up about 24% of the fund as of Jan. 7. All six were still among its 10 biggest holdings as of Oct. 13. Texas Instruments, the fund's largest position, has risen around 61% this year. The two oil producers have gained about 56% and 49%, the two drugmakers about 40% and 37%, and Coca-Cola about 36%.

Writing for the options data platform, Brett Friedman noted that energy has understandably attracted the most attention in 2026.

However, the three agricultural commodities have delivered with much less fanfare. They also hold meaningful weights in the S&P GSCI and the Bloomberg Commodity Index.

For context, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY) and Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) had returned 11.7% and 15.8% year-to-date, respectively, as of Oct. 16.

Meanwhile, the 2026 year-to-date cumulative performance for sugar stands at +44.7%; for Chicago SRW wheat it is +32.3%, and for soybeans it is +22.1%

Friedman said the performance of the three crops is even more impressive on a Sharpe ratio basis (sugar +1.72%, soybeans +1.3% and Chicago SRW wheat +1.2%), which measures returns relative to volatility.

Unsure what to buy ahead of earnings? Our AI's recent pre-earnings calls delivered gains of +77% to +118% after results dropped. See this month's earnings picks »

Wheat and soybeans have moved almost in lockstep this year. Their calendar-year price correlation stands at a record 0.919, meaning roughly 85% of the price movement in one crop can be explained by the other.

That leaves minimal diversification benefit between them. Both, however, continue to show their usual seasonal implied volatility pattern.

Copper, by contrast, has been caught up in the attention around AI given its role as a key input for electronics.

"Regardless, those trading it as an AI proxy have been disappointed so far this year," Friedman wrote.

Copper has returned 15.5% year to date, but its Sharpe ratio is only 0.65, lower than sugar, soybeans and wheat. Its average implied volatility of 29.1% this year remains above its 21-year baseline of 26.9%.

"The financial press often confuses a compelling narrative with actual, risk-adjusted results," Friedman said.

An Actively Managed ETF With Nasdaq-100 Exposure That Seeks Weekly Income From Put Credit Spreads and Uses a Short-Dated Options Hedge Each Trading Day

Tuttle Capital Management (TCM), a leading issuer of thematic and rules-based ETFs, today announced the launch of the Tuttle Capital Innovation 100 Income and Hedge ETF (CBOE: QQDH), an actively managed ETF that seeks current income and, secondarily, long-term capital appreciation.

QQDH holds exposure to the Nasdaq-100® Index mainly through the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ), with at least 80% of net assets in QQQ or options that use QQQ or the index as a reference asset. It does not write call options over that exposure, so the exposure is not capped at a covered-call strike.

To seek income, the Fund sells put credit spreads.The Fund seeks to provide

Nasdaq-100 exposure while employing options strategies designed to generate income and manage risk. There is no guarantee that distributions will be made.

Each business day, the Fund seeks to put on a hedge using options that expire the next trading day. The hedge is designed principally for short, sharp declines. It may not help in a gradual decline and can add to losses in a modest one.

The Fund's total annual operating expense ratio is 0.95% and lists on [Exchange] under the ticker QQDH.

Riverside, Connecticut--(Newsfile Corp. - October 23, 2026) - Tuttle Capital Management, LLC, a leading issuer of thematic and rules-based ETFs, today announced the launch of the Tuttle Capital Innovation 100 Income and Hedge ETF ([Exchange]: QQDH). QQDH is an actively managed ETF that combines exposure to the Nasdaq-100® Index, through the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ) and/or options, with two separate options overlays: an income strategy built on put credit spreads and a daily hedging strategy built on short-dated put ratio backspreads.

"Many income ETFs generate income by writing calls, which can cap the upside of what they hold," said Matthew Tuttle, Chief Executive Officer of Tuttle Capital Management and portfolio manager of the Fund. "QQDH takes a different route: we don't write calls over the Nasdaq-100 exposure, we seek income with put credit spreads instead, and we reset a hedge every day. Each of those pieces can lose money, and investors should understand all three before they own the fund."

How QQDH Is Built
QQDH has three parts: long exposure to the Nasdaq-100® Index, an income overlay, and a daily hedge.

The Long Exposure
QQDH holds its exposure mainly through the Invesco QQQ Trust (QQQ). It can also build that exposure with options, by buying a call and selling a put with about the same strike price and expiration date. That combination generally rises and falls with QQQ, though not identically.

Goldman Sachs prime brokerage data first reported on Thursday, October 22, 2026, shows hedge funds have built short positions in stocks to a near five-year high. Major indexes moved in opposite directions that same day.

Shutterstock

The S&P 500 fell 93.74 points, or 1.21%, to 7,663.43. The Nasdaq Composite dropped 694 points, or 2.6%, to 26,008.86. The Dow added 11.89 points to 52,867.98, and the Russell 2000 gained 0.1%.

The SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSEARCA:SPY) closed at $763.96, down 1.18%. The Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) fell 2.86% to $704.47.

Heavy shorting can mean professionals expect more downside. It also leaves the market full of sellers who will eventually have to buy shares back, and those positions are concentrated in tech stocks.

How Bearish Hedge Funds Have Become

In October, short sales exceeded long purchases across global stocks by about five-to-one. Short leverage in Goldman's prime book has reached the 99th percentile of its five-year history, "indicating bearish exposure was higher than in almost all of that period."

Net leverage (longs minus shorts) among fundamental long-short funds is near a three-year low, while gross leverage (longs plus shorts) has risen. That means funds are adding risk on both sides of their books and leaning bearish overall.

Goldman's Mark Wilson described net equity exposure as historically low amid swings in rates and energy prices. He said higher yields pushed investors to rethink equity risk.

"The Big Short" investor Michael Burry's growing Substack audience and upcoming fee increases could lift its annual revenue potential above $232 million — more than double July's levels — as he turned the spotlight on four "busted" stocks that could offer shelter in a prolonged bear market.

The investor highlighted Adobe (ADBE), Fiserv (FISV), Birkenstock (BIRK) and QXO as pockets of strength during Thursday's technology selloff, while separately flagging a possible accounting risk for Nvidia (NVDA).

Burry Raises Rates As His Audience Tops 342,000

Burry said Cassandra Unchained's monthly subscription would rise from $49 to $69, while the annual fee would increase from $479 to $679. The changes take effect from Nov.1, implying increases of over 40% in both time periods. "Subscribe before the end of the month, and you will keep the lower rate for the life of your subscription," he said on X.

His official subscription page now shows more than 342,000 subscribers, compared with 300,044 in July, marking growth of about 14%. At $679 per annual subscription, 342,000 subscriptions would generate $232.2 million in annual gross revenue, which is about 104% above July's $113.7 million estimate by Stocktwits, which used 300,044 subscribers and a $379 annual fee.

However, the $232.2 million figure comes with a catch: it assumes every subscriber pays the new annual fee. Burry's audience includes free readers, while existing subscribers can keep lower rates. His actual revenue and paid-subscriber count are currently undisclosed.

How $232M Stacks Up Against Wall Street's Biggest Winners

Even picking the S&P 500's 10 biggest winners this year would deliver gains far below l $232.2 million. Investing $1 million in each would turn $10 million into about $34.2 million, a $24.2 million gain, with the newsletter figure about 9.6 times higher.
